commentary.hc2:
Headline CPI ran at 4.08% YoY in October 2026, well above the 2.87% core reading, with the gap driven entirely by energy. Electricity surged 47.25% YoY and gasoline 37.36% YoY, pulling the all-items figure sharply higher while core goods and services remained comparatively contained. Shelter held at 3.54% YoY, motor vehicle insurance turned negative on a 12-month basis at -4.39% despite a 0.71% monthly uptick, and used vehicles continued to deflate at -3.31% YoY, acting as modest offsets within core.

• Tire industry: The 37.36% YoY gasoline surge and 47.25% YoY electricity spike raise operating costs across the supply chain and compress fleet operators' margins, which typically delays discretionary tire replacement cycles and pressures volume demand even as the 6.45% YoY rise in motor vehicle maintenance & repair signals continued consumer spending on essential vehicle upkeep.
commentary.mfg2:
Electricity costs rose sharply at +47.25% year-over-year in October 2026, far outpacing the other components. Natural gas increased modestly at +5.14%, while Food at Home and Household Furnishings posted comparatively mild gains of +2.22% and +1.78%, respectively. The spread between the highest and lowest components spans roughly 45 percentage points, with electricity as a clear outlier against an otherwise subdued inflationary backdrop in goods and other energy inputs.

• Tire industry: Electricity's 47.25% surge materially raises the operating cost of energy-intensive tire manufacturing processes—including mixing, curing, and vulcanization—compressing plant-level margins unless absorbed through pricing or offset by efficiency gains.
commentary.transp2:
Gasoline prices rose 37.36% year-over-year in October 2026, representing the sharpest increase among the tracked components. Airline fares followed with a 22.94% gain, while fuel oil posted a comparatively modest 3.71% increase. Motor vehicle insurance was the sole component to decline, falling 4.39% over the same period.

• Tire industry: The 37.36% surge in gasoline costs raises fleet operators' total cost of ownership substantially, which historically accelerates evaluation of fuel-efficiency improvements including tire rolling-resistance upgrades and load optimization to offset fuel expenditure.
commentary.fed2:
Headline CPI is running 208 basis points above the 2% target, while core at 2.87% indicates that underlying price pressures remain elevated even after stripping out food and energy. The 0.35% monthly gain, if sustained, annualizes to roughly 4.3%, well above the target run rate. The gap between headline and core suggests energy or food components are amplifying the top-line reading, though core itself has not returned to target-consistent levels. Taken together, the data does not yet provide the Fed with the confidence it has stated it needs to ease policy; the dual elevation in both headline and core measures keeps the threshold for rate cuts high and extends the period in which a restrictive stance remains justifiable.

• Tire industry: Persistently elevated inflation and the associated higher-for-longer rate environment raise borrowing costs on capital-intensive manufacturing and fleet financing, while sustained price pressure in upstream petrochemical and synthetic-rubber inputs continues to compress margin management options.
commentary.lens2:
Energy costs dominate the October 2026 inflation picture, with headline CPI running at 4.08% year-over-year while core remains considerably more contained at 2.87%, indicating that the gap is driven by commodity price swings rather than broad demand-side overheating.

• Electricity is the single most acute pressure point, up 47.25% year-over-year and still accelerating at 2.42% month-over-month; gasoline (+37.36% YoY / +1.04% MoM) and airline fares (+22.94% YoY) compound the energy-and-transport cluster, suggesting fuel costs are transmitting rapidly into movement-of-people pricing.

• Goods disinflation is visible in vehicle-related categories: new vehicle prices are nearly flat (+0.74% YoY), used cars and trucks are actively deflating (-3.31% YoY / -1.22% MoM), and motor vehicle insurance has turned negative on an annual basis (-4.39% YoY), partly offsetting energy-driven headline pressure on household budgets.

• Services and shelter costs are running at a moderate but persistent pace—shelter at +3.54% YoY and motor vehicle maintenance & repair at +6.45% YoY—indicating labor-intensive categories have not fully unwound their post-pandemic pricing even as goods prices soften.

• Tire industry: With gasoline up 37% year-over-year and electricity costs surging, fleet operators and consumers face sharply higher total vehicle operating costs, which historically compresses discretionary vehicle spending and can delay tire
commentary.tire2:
**Auto & Tire CPI Channel — October 2026**

• New vehicle prices rose 0.74% year-over-year, a modest gain consistent with broadly stable transaction prices, while used vehicle prices fell 3.31%, continuing the multi-year normalization from post-pandemic peaks and compressing the price spread between new and used inventory.

• Motor vehicle maintenance & repair inflation ran at 6.45% year-over-year, the sharpest move in the channel, reflecting sustained elevation in labor costs and parts pricing at the service level even as upstream vehicle prices softened.

• Motor vehicle insurance declined 4.39% year-over-year, reversing a prolonged period of double-digit premium increases; lower used-vehicle replacement values and moderating claims costs are consistent with this directional shift.

---

• **Tire industry:** The 6.45% surge in motor vehicle maintenance & repair CPI signals that end consumers are absorbing higher service and parts costs, supporting sustained demand and pricing power for replacement tires sold through the aftermarket service channel.
commentary.ppi2:
Final demand producer prices rose 6.52% year-over-year and 0.35% month-over-month in October 2026.

Goods inflation is running well ahead of services: final demand goods were up 10.25% YoY, driven in large part by energy (+36.85% YoY), while final demand services rose 4.97% YoY, with transportation and warehousing the standout component at +18.50% YoY and +2.04% MoM. Core goods (less foods and energy) advanced 5.21% YoY, and the broadest core measure stripping out trade services held at 4.86% YoY, suggesting underlying price pressure is not confined to volatile categories. On the pipeline, processed goods for intermediate demand were up 14.47% YoY and unprocessed goods 17.05% YoY—both running materially above final demand headline—indicating that upstream cost pressure has not yet fully passed through to finished-goods prices.

For tire-relevant inputs, synthetic rubber rose 11.26% YoY (NSA), and the broader rubber and plastic products index was up 5.81% YoY (NSA), while finished tires and tubes increased only 1.59% YoY (NSA) and passenger car tires 2.56% Y
commentary.ppilens2:
Synthetic rubber producer prices rose 11.26% year-over-year in October 2026, outpacing all other segments in the tire-input cost stack by a wide margin.

• Synthetic rubber (NSA, YoY): +11.26%, the sharpest increase across the stack and the dominant upstream pressure on tire manufacturing costs.
• Passenger car tires (NSA, YoY): +2.56%; tires & tubes (NSA, YoY): +1.59%—both finished-tire categories show increases considerably below the synthetic rubber input rate, indicating that the upstream cost pressure has not passed through fully to finished tire prices at the producer level.
• Rubber & plastics products (NSA, YoY): +5.81%, sitting between the raw synthetic rubber figure and the finished tire figures, consistent with partial absorption or blending of cost pressures across the broader rubber and plastics manufacturing segment.

The spread between the synthetic rubber input price (+11.26%) and finished passenger car tire prices (+2.56%) stands at roughly 870 basis points, suggesting margin compression or offsetting efficiencies elsewhere in the production process. Tires & tubes at +1.59% show an even wider gap against the synthetic rubber input, at nearly 970 basis points.

• Tire industry: With synthetic rubber running more than four times the rate of finished tire price inflation, tire and transportation-equipment manufacturers face meaningful margin pressure on the input side unless natural rubber sourcing, compounding substitution, or supply contract structures provide sufficient offset.
